Rebuilding the Hack Pack IDE to turn first time coders into repeat hackers.

CrunchLabs teaches kids and beginners to code through build it yourself robot kits, but once the box was unpacked, the digital experience meant to keep hackers engaged was falling flat.

0 → 1 From an open-ended brief to a defined product direction

Team

01 / The Challenge

Started broad, got specific.

CrunchLabs came to us without a fixed brief, just a wide spread of ideas and no shared sense of priority. That made this true 0 → 1 product work: before we could design anything, we had to define what the product should become and what success would actually mean.

We jumped into research with heuristic and competitive evaluations before moving into onsite collaborations at the CrunchLabs Headquarters in a super cool, undisclosed location, where they also happen to film a lot of videos! When we were onsite, we talked about what was actually feasible for developers and aligned with the goals of the company. We also looked at success criteria, any resources needed and potential challenges with our partner Trey and the Hack Pack toy designers.

Short term goal

Position the IDE as a tool to increase user retention.

The business focus is to improve the UI, gather data on how people use the IDE, and improve retention and engagement through a better IDE experience today.

Long term goal

Teach more users how to code through fun, approachable experiences.

More aspirational in nature: teach more people to code in fun, approachable ways, true to CrunchLabs' mission of showing kids and kids at heart how to Think Like an Engineer.

02 / The Problem

The IDE was "good enough," and that was the problem.

We combined a survey, unmoderated usability tests and live interviews to see what the numbers weren't telling us.

38
Survey responses

38 Hack Pack subscribers rated the current IDE on a Likert scale.

38
Unmoderated tests

38 asynchronous tests with users on the current IDE.

6
Live interviews

6 moderated, semi-structured interviews with users on our initial design.

25
Final prototype tests

25 asynchronous tests with users on the final design.

Designing with kidsWorking with a younger user group shaped how we ran every study: it changed how we worded questions and how we sourced participants, and every tester was required and screened to meet age requirements.

Using a Likert scale in our survey of 38 Hack Pack subscribers, we found the IDE wasn't broken:

71%
mostly or fully understood how the IDE worked
77%
were interested or very interested in using it again
PAIN POINT 01

Unfocused interface

Heavy coding jargon alienated beginners, and the level system felt redundant, and most users skipped straight to Level 3.

“I never got the point of Level 1 or 2. They always seem exactly the same.”Participant 3, Intermediate CoderModerated Semi-Structured Interview
PAIN POINT 02

No context on errors

The IDE gave little explanation when something broke, leaving beginners stuck without knowing why.

“It’s fun to see how [my kids] work out their frustrations […] But I would like some explanation of errors to save some frustration though.”Participant 6, Beginner CoderModerated Semi-Structured Interview
PAIN POINT 03

Community engagement is lacking

A hidden Discord channel was the only community resource to understand and share with other hackers. Parents also flagged this as a safety concern, limiting younger users from engaging with and sharing exciting hacks.

“The IDE itself is fine to use… but there really needs to be a repository for other hacks.”Participant 1, Advanced CoderModerated Semi-Structured Interview
03 / The Solution : Parts List

From first compile to first share.

Rather than patching the IDE in isolation, we designed six features that follow a hacker's whole journey: learning the tools, fixing mistakes, celebrating a win, organizing their work, and finding their next idea.

Guided & Advanced Mode

Feature 01

The problem

Users couldn’t tell what Levels 1–3 meant. The system felt redundant, and most users skipped straight to Level 3.

What we built

Two modes, “Guided” and “Advanced,” replace the vague “Level 1, Level 2, Level 3.” Guided is geared toward beginners, Advanced toward experienced coders. This lowers the barrier for entry, making the IDE more accessible to new coders and building confidence before they move to a full code editor.

What we heard

GUIDED / ADVANCED TOGGLE, REPLACING LEVELS 1–3

Bug Squasher

Feature 02

The problem

The IDE gave little explanation when something broke, leaving beginners stuck without knowing why.

What we built

A built-in assistant that scans code for potential syntax and compilation errors. It helps users identify coding mistakes and encourages independent problem-solving with relevant coding concepts, increasing retention and adoption of the IDE.

What we heard

BUG SQUASHER: PLAIN LANGUAGE EXPLANATION

Success Feedback

Feature 03

What we built

A confirmation pop-up when a user’s code successfully compiles, providing clearer visual feedback that the step is complete and reducing user frustration.

SUCCESS FEEDBACK: UPLOAD TO ROBOT + CONFIRMATION

File Explorer 2.0

Feature 04

What we built

A reimagined file explorer that gives new and experienced users a more organized place to tinker: a real workspace to duplicate projects, import code and experiment. It keeps experienced users engaged longer and tinkering more.

In final testing

82%found File Explorer very or extremely useful
95.7%understood file actions immediately
FILE EXPLORER 2.0: CREATE, IMPORT, NEW FILE

Community Hacks Hub

Feature 05

The problem

A hidden Discord channel was the only place to find and share hacks, and parents flagged it as a safety concern.

What we built

A centralized home for user built and CrunchLabs original hacks, each highlighted with media, required hardware and key coding concepts, where today it all lives in Discord channels. Hackers find inspiration from peers, come back more often, and grow a culture of creativity around hacking.

What we heard

In final testing

91%said they would visit Community Hacks
COMMUNITY HACKS HUB: LANDING + HACK DETAIL

Hack Universe

Feature 06

What we built

Ties the IDE, Community Hacks, and future features into one connected space. Tested two directions, and 75% of users preferred this one.

In final testing

75%preferred this direction over the alternative we tested
HACK UNIVERSE: MAP + KIT DETAIL

04 / Testing & Validation

Did users actually like it?

We ran 25 unmoderated tests on the final prototypes and measured them against the original, preexisting product, using the same Likert scale questions from our first round of testing.

The number that mattered mostIn our first round we asked users how likely they were to use the current IDE again. In our final round we asked the same question about our redesign. Here's how many said “extremely likely” to using the redesigned IDE versus the preexisting IDE.
